disposition_reason: Japanese retail survey measuring Cd by ICP-MS in 180 chocolate products (140 dark, 35 milk, 5 white) and 140 cocoa powder products, with per-product values, group summary statistics and cocoa-solids bins.
disposition_locator: Materials and Methods (Samples), p.269-270; Tables 2-5, p.271-273

study.material_scope: retail dark, milk and white chocolate; retail cocoa powder products
study.growing_origin_vs_market: Purchase market: online or supermarkets in Tokyo and surrounding areas, Japan. Cocoa growing origin not reported.
study.sampling_unit: individual retail products (one homogenised portion per product)
study.method: ICP-MS (Thermo iCAP Q) after closed-vessel microwave digestion (0.5 g, HNO3 + H2O2), In internal standard
study.lod_loq: Cd LOQ 0.00005 mg/kg (0.05 ug/kg); no LOD stated
study.basis: as sold (homogenised product; no moisture or fat correction reported)
study.qa: In-house validation with chocolate spiked at 0.005, 0.2 and 1.0 mg/kg over 5 days: trueness 101-103%, repeatability RSD 1.3-4.1%, intralaboratory reproducibility RSD 1.3-5.3% (Table 1). Blank digests per vessel. No CRM reported.

findings.material: Chocolate products, total (dark+milk+white)
findings.basis: as sold (homogenised retail product; no drying or fat-free correction reported)
findings.notes: Table 3 summary statistics; recomputed from Table 2/4 per-product values and reconciled within rounding. Total minimum 0.00021 mg/kg is a white chocolate product.
findings.integrity_issue: Results text states "The Cd concentrations detected in the white chocolate products were all below the limit of quantitation", but the stated LOQ is 0.00005 mg/kg and all five white chocolate values in Table 2 (0.00021-0.00158 mg/kg) are above it; values are kept as printed.

contradictions_with_stored_summary: Stored summary does not mention that the Results text says white chocolate values were all below the LOQ, which conflicts with the printed white chocolate values and the stated LOQ of 0.00005 mg/kg.

Stored summary describes Table 5 as the 140 labelled products without noting that the five white chocolates also carry labelled cocoa solids (28-35%) in Table 2 and were excluded; 145 of 180 products actually have a labelled cocoa percentage.
unresolved: Exceedance counts (8/180 chocolate, 26/140 cocoa powder) are the authors' comparison of 2015-2016 products against EU MLs effective 2019; two chocolate exceedances (Nos. 17 and 32) are "possible nonconformity" based on an assumed <50% cocoa solids where the label gave none.
Whether cocoa powder products are natural or alkalised, and whether any are sweetened drinking-chocolate powders, is not reported.
Brand and growing origin of products are not reported; values are product-level only (no lot replication).
